slides.title: Sensors in Robotics
slides.text:
Sensors in Robotics
•  Robot sensors are devices that enable robots to perceive,
  measure, and interact with their environment or internal state,
  mimicking human senses like sight, hearing, and touch.
•  In robotics, sensors act as the eyes, ears, and skin of the system by
   collecting real-time information about physical conditions such as
   distance, position, motion, light, and orientation.
•  Without sensors, a robot cannot make intelligent
   decisions or operate autonomously.





                                                                                                           3

visualInspection.notes: All three bullets viewed. Sensors observe environment or internal state and deliver physical-condition information. The absolute claim that robots cannot operate autonomously without sensors needs a bounded interpretation: open-loop programmed behavior can exist, but adaptation to unobserved changes is unsupported.

slides.title: Role of Sensors in a Robotic System
slides.text:
Role of Sensors in a Robotic System

•  Convert physical parameters (distance, speed, acceleration, light, etc.)
   into electrical signals.
•  Perception: Understand the environmental state
•  Control: Enable closed-loop control for accuracy and stability.
•  Safety: Help the robot sense obstacles, navigate, and adapt to
   changing environments.
•  Learning: Feed data to AI/ML algorithms
•  Localization: Know where the robot is in space.
•  Manipulation: Grasp, push, pull with precision.
•  Sensors are the interface between the robot and the
   physical world


                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Transduction and all six roles viewed: perception, closed-loop control, safety, learning, localization, manipulation. Sensors provide evidence, not an automatic guarantee of stability or safety.

slides.title: Key Sensor Performance Characteristics
slides.text:
Key Sensor Performance Characteristics

•  Range: Minimum and maximum values the sensor can measure reliably.
•  Span: Maximum value – minimum value.
•   Error: measured value – true value.
•  Resolution: Smallest change in input that the sensor can detect.
•  Accuracy: Closeness of the measured value to the true value.
•  Precision: Repeatability — consistency of readings under the same conditions.
•  Dead Band: range of input values for which no output.
•  Dead Time: length of time from the application of an
   input until the output begins to respond to the change.
•  Sensor bandwidth (Hz): the range of frequencies
   over which a sensor can accurately measure and
   detect changes in a physical condition.



                                                                                                           6

visualInspection.notes: All definitions viewed: range endpoints; span=max-min; signed error=measured-true; resolution; accuracy; repeatability/precision; dead band; dead time; bandwidth Hz. Dead band wording no output is shorthand for no response/change, not necessarily zero signal. Distinguish bandwidth from sample/update rate and dead time from overall latency.

slides.title: •  Latency: the delay between a physical event and the availability of
slides.text:
•  Latency: the delay between a physical event and the availability of
   sensor output.
•  Sensitivity: Relationship indicating how much output one gets per unit
   input.
•  Hysteresis Error: Different output for the same value of the input,
   depending upon whether it has been obtained for an increasing value or
   for a decreasing value.
•  Linearity: Proportionality of output to input
   across the measurement range.
•  Noise: Random variation superimposed on the
   true signal value.



                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: All five definitions viewed: latency, output-per-input sensitivity, direction-dependent hysteresis, linearity, random noise. Proportionality wording is a simplified linearity definition; an affine calibration may include offset. Distinguish bias, noise and hysteresis; sensitivity has output/input units.

slides.title: Potentiometer (Position Sensor)
slides.text:
Potentiometer (Position Sensor)

•  Definition
   – A potentiometer is an analog variable resistor used to measure angular or linear
        position.
•  Working Principle
   – A potentiometer has three terminals: Vcc, GND, and Wiper.
   – When the shaft rotates, the wiper moves along a resistive track.
   –  This changes the output voltage proportionally.
   – Arduino reads this voltage using its ADC (Analog to Digital Converter).
•  Applications in Robotics
   – Robotic arm joint angle sensing
   – Servo calibration
   – Manual control interfaces
   – Feedback in closed-loop systems      Rotary Potentiometer
                                            Source: https://www.build-electronic-circuits.com/

                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Every bullet and rotary component photo viewed. Three terminal divider uses supply, ground and wiper; linear track and negligible loading are needed for voltage proportional to position. ADC reads voltage, not angle without calibration. All four applications preserved.

slides.title: Encoder (Rotary Encoder)
slides.text:
Encoder (Rotary Encoder)

•  Definition
   – An encoder converts mechanical motion
       into digital signals, allowing robots to
      measure speed, direction, and position.
•  Types                                                                Four bit
                                                                             absolute   – Incremental Encoder: Generates pulses per
                                                                      encoder
       revolution; needs a reference home
       position on startup; Common in servo
      motors
   – Absolute Encoder: Outputs a unique code
        for every shaft position; retains state after
       power-off; and is used in robotic arms.



                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: Both diagrams inspected: optical transmitter/slotted disk/receiver; four concentric absolute tracks with sixteen binary labels 0000 through1111. Four-bit example is binary labeling, not automatically Gray code. Incremental pulses need reference for absolute position; single-turn absolute angle after power-up does not automatically preserve multi-turn history.

slides.title: Obstacle Avoidance Sensor (IR)
slides.text:
Obstacle Avoidance Sensor (IR)

•  Definition
   – An Infrared (IR) obstacle sensor detects objects by emitting infrared light and
       measuring the reflected radiation from nearby surfaces.
•  Working Principle
   –  IR LED emits infrared radiation.
   – Radiation strikes an obstacle.
   – Reflected IR is received by a photodiode or phototransistor.
   –  Signal strength changes based on distance.
   – Comparator converts analog signal into digital output.
•  Applications
   –  Line follower robots
   – Obstacle avoiding robots
   – Edge detection


                                                                                                          15

visualInspection.notes: All bullets and diagram rays viewed. IR LED sends light toward surface, photodiode receives reflection; intensity fed to comparator produces digital classification. Reflectivity/angle/ambient light affect signal as well as distance; digital threshold is not a calibrated range value. Three applications line-following, obstacle avoidance and edge detection.

slides.title: Light Dependent Resistor
slides.text:
Light Dependent Resistor

•  Definition
   – An LDR (Light Dependent Resistor) is a sensor whose resistance changes with
         light intensity.
•  Working Principle
   –  Bright light → low resistance
   – Low light → high resistance
   – Used in voltage divider circuit
   – Arduino reads voltage change

                                              Source: https://how2electronics.com/•  Applications in Robotics
   –  Line-following robots
   – Automatic street-light robots
   –  Solar tracking robots
   – Obstacle detection (light-based)


                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: All text and component labels inspected. Bright illumination reduces resistance; dim light increases it. Decreasing schematic graph has resistance in ohms and illumination in lux over multiple decades, but does not establish a universal reciprocal law or precise intermediate calibration. Diagram labels electrodes, clear coating, photoconductive material, cold-weld contacts, ceramic and wire terminals. Applications include line following, street lights, solar tracking and light-based detection.

slides.title: Switch Sensors – Tilt Switch
slides.text:
Switch Sensors – Tilt Switch

•  Definition
   – A tilt switch detects angular
     movement or orientation.
•  Working Principle
   – Contains a metal ball
   –  Ball closes circuit when tilted
•  Applications                   Source: https://www.instructables.com/
   – Fall-detection robots
   – Orientation sensing
   – Safety shutdown systems


                                                                                                          23

visualInspection.notes: Both metal-ball tube sketches viewed. One position leaves the two contacts open; tilted drawing lets ball bridge them. Two pins A/B, tilt arrow and ball positions are visible. Binary contact indicates a threshold state, not a continuous angle; mounting and acceleration matter. Applications fall detection, orientation and safety shutdown require a larger control system.

slides.title: Ultrasonic Sensor — Sound-Based Ranging
slides.text:
Ultrasonic Sensor — Sound-Based Ranging

•  Definition
    –  An active distance-measuring sensor that determines the distance between the robot and an
         object by transmitting ultrasonic sound waves and receiving their reflected echo.
    –   It is non-contact, low-cost, and widely used in mobile robotics.
    –  Works in fog, dust, darkness
    –  Affected by temperature & wind; Limited range: ~0.02–4 m typical
•  Working Principle
    –  The controller sends a trigger pulse to the sensor.
    –  The sensor emits ultrasonic waves at a frequency of 40 kHz.
    –  These waves propagate through the air until they strike an object.
    –  The waves are reflected back toward the sensor.
    –  The echo pin remains HIGH for the duration of the wave’s round trip.
    –  The microcontroller calculates distance using the travel time.
    –  Distance Formula: Distance = (Time × Speed of Sound) / 2
    –  Speed of sound in air ≈ 343 m/s


                                                                                                          31

visualInspection.notes: All bullets/formula and transmitter/receiver echo diagram inspected. Active non-contact40kHz example, echo-high duration for round trip, d=tc/2 with c≈343m/s. Typical0.02–4m range is example-specific, not universal. Temperature and wind matter; works in darkness/fog/dust is not environmental immunity.

slides.title: LiDAR - Light Detection and Ranging Sensor (VL53L0X)
slides.text:
LiDAR - Light Detection and Ranging Sensor (VL53L0X)

•  LiDAR is a laser-based distance sensing technology that measures
   distance by calculating the time taken by a laser pulse to return after
   reflecting from an object.
•  LiDAR emits laser pulses and measures the Time-of-Flight (ToF) of
   returning photons to build 2D or 3D point clouds of the environment.
•  Each laser “shot” gives you
   – The distance to a surface point (from time-of-flight).
   – The direction of the beam when that shot was
      taken (scan angles and sensor pose).
•  From these, the system computes a 2D/3D
   coordinate for each return, and the collection of all
   such points forms the point cloud.



                                                                                                          45

visualInspection.notes: All text inspected. Header namesVL53L0X while body describes general scanning LiDAR and point clouds. Range plus beam direction/scan angles and sensor pose allow coordinates; a single-zone fixed VL53L0X does not itself provide a rotating2D/3D cloud. Distinguish general ToF principle from product capabilities.

slides.title: •  Working Principle
slides.text:
•  Working Principle
    – A laser diode emits a short light pulse; Pulse travels at the speed of light.
    –  Pulse strikes an object and reflects back.
    –  Photodetector captures reflected light.
    –  Sensor calculates Time of Flight (ToF)
    –  Distance = (Time × Speed of light) / 2
    – Speed of light = 3 × 108 m/s
•   2D LiDAR
    –  Single rotating laser plane (e.g. SICK, Hokuyo)           Source: https://lastminuteengineers.com/
    –  360° scan; range 0.1–40 m; ~10–40 Hz
    – Used for obstacle avoidance, floor mapping
•  3D LiDAR
    –  Multiple stacked laser channels (Velodyne 64-beam)
    –  Full 3D point cloud; 100k–2M pts/s
    – Used in autonomous vehicles, drone mapping

                                                                                                          46

visualInspection.notes: Formula d=tc/2,c=3×10^8m/s; emission/reflection/photodetection diagram. 2D single rotating plane, example360degrees,0.1–40m,10–40Hz;3D multiple channels example64beam,100k–2Mpoints/s. These ranges/rates are illustrative device-class values, not VL53L0X specs or universal sensor limits.

slides.title: Vision Sensors — Camera Types in Robotics
slides.text:
Vision Sensors — Camera Types in Robotics

•  Monocular
   –  Single lens; compact & cheap. Lacks native depth. Used with depth estimation
         AI.
•   Stereo
   – Two cameras; compute disparity map for 3D reconstruction. Reliable up to ~5m.
•  RGB-D
   – Combines colour + depth (e.g. Intel RealSense, Kinect). Direct per-pixel depth.
•   Fisheye/360°
   – Ultra-wide FOV (>180°). Used in parking, UAVs, and SLAM.
•  Thermal IR
   – Detects heat signatures; works in darkness. Used in
          fire, security, and medical.
•  Event Camera
   – Neuromorphic; outputs pixel-level brightness
       changes async. <1 ms latency.




                                                                                                          53

visualInspection.notes: Six modality rows inspected: monocular lacks native depth,stereo disparity,RGB-D,color+depth,fisheye/360ultrawide,thermalIR,asynchronous event brightness change. Approx5m stereo reliability,<1ms event latency,>180degreeFOV are illustrative not universal guarantees. RGB-D can have invalid/unregistered pixels. Thermal is emitted heat signature, not active reflectiveIR obstacle module.

slides.title: CAMERA SENSOR
slides.text:
CAMERA SENSOR

•  Definition
    – A camera sensor is an electronic device inside a digital camera that captures light and
        converts it into electrical signals, which are then processed to create a digital image.
•  Working Principle
    –  Light from a scene passes through the lens and hits the camera sensor.
    –  The sensor is made up of millions of tiny light-sensitive elements called pixels (photodiodes).Each
          pixel detects the intensity of light falling on it.
    –  Each pixel converts light energy into an electrical charge. More light equal to stronger electrical
           signal.
    –  Since pixels only measure light intensity, a color filter array
          (usually Bayer filter: Red, Green, Blue) is placed over them to
         capture color information.
    –  The electrical signals are converted into digital data using an
          Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC).
    –  The camera processor then forms the final image.


                                                                                                          54

visualInspection.notes: Every working-principle bullet viewed. Lens→photodiode charge→colorfilter sampling→ADC→processor image. More light stronger signal assumes fixed exposure/gain and unsaturated response. Bayer RGB described but no actual2×2 pattern shown; any numeric Bayer mosaic premise must be explicitly supplied. Not every camera requires Bayer or millions of pixels.

•  Example: Image Processing with YOLOv8 for Object Detection
    YOLOv8 (You Only Look Once version 8) is a deep learning model used for real-time
    object detection.
     In object detection using YOLOv8:
            1.  The camera captures an image.
            2.  The image is processed using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).
            3.  The model detects objects in the image.
            4.    It draws bounding boxes around detected objects.
            5.    It displays object names with confidence scores

    can detect and label objects like person, car, bicycle, bus,
     etc., in real time.

Real-time is performance aspiration not guaranteed by CPUlarge model. Bounding box is2D localization, not metric3D position; confidence is model score not guaranteed probability or dataset precision.

slides.title: DEPTH CAMERA (INTEL REALSENSE D415)
slides.text:
DEPTH CAMERA (INTEL REALSENSE D415)

•   Definition
    – A Depth Camera is a vision sensor that captures distance (depth) information of
        objects in a scene in addition to normal color images. Unlike a regular camera that
        only captures 2D images, a depth camera can understand the 3D structure of the
       environment.
•  Working Principle
    –  Stereo Vision Method, uses two cameras placed side by side
    –  Captures two images of the same object
    –  Calculates depth by finding the difference (disparity) between the images
•  A depth camera provides multiple outputs:
 1.  RGB Image – Normal color image, Used for object recognition
     Depth Map – Each pixel of 2D image contains a distance value
 2.   Point Cloud Data – 3D coordinates (X, Y, Z) of each pixel
 3.   Infrared Image – Raw infrared data used for depth calculation



                                                                                                          60

slides.title: Force & Torque Sensors in Robot Manipulation
slides.text:
Force & Torque Sensors in Robot Manipulation

•   6-axis F/T sensors at robot wrists measure three forces (Fx, Fy, Fz) and three moments
   (Mx, My, Mz), enabling compliant control and safe human-robot collaboration.
•   Strain Gauge F/T
    – Wheatstone bridge of bonded gauges
    –  High resolution; sub-mN sensitivity
    –  Susceptible to temperature drift
•   Piezoelectric F/T
    – Charge proportional to applied force
    –  Excellent dynamic response (>10 kHz)
    – Not suited for static/DC loads (drift)
•   Capacitive F/T
    –  Capacitance changes with deflection
    – Low noise; good for soft robotics
    – Used in tactile array sensors

slides.title: How to Select the Right Sensor
slides.text:
How to Select the Right Sensor

•   Define the Measurement Need
    – What physical quantity must be measured? What range, resolution, and update rate does
        the task require?
•   Consider Operating Environment
    –  Indoor vs. outdoor? Temperature extremes? Dust, moisture, vibration? Lighting
        conditions (camera)?
•   Interface & Computational Load
    –  I²C / SPI / UART / Ethernet / CAN? Processing latency budget? Edge vs. cloud inference for
        AI models?
•   Size, Weight & Power
    –  Critical for UAVs and wearables. Total sensor power budget constrains fleet endurance.
•   Cost vs. Redundancy
    –  Quantify the risk of sensor failure. Use multiple cheap sensors
         vs. one expensive redundant sensor?
•   Calibration & Maintenance
    – How often must the sensor be recalibrated?
       Are in-field calibration methods available?
